211.title: The light in the sun
211.hook: Krishna says the light in sun, fire and every body is his; why Hindus chant before meals
211.carry: the divine light is seated in every heart
211.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant Gita 15.14, 'aham vaishvanaro bhutva', before meals, often after 4.24, 'brahmarpanam'; some families and communities recite the whole of chapter fifteen before eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashvattha: the world of change as an upside-down fig, cut with the axe of not clinging. Today, light.

The power goes out at night. The fridge goes quiet, the screen goes black. Someone finds a candle and strikes a match, and a small flame fills the room. Outside, the moon is lighting the street. And the whole time, without anyone noticing, a body keeps its own quiet warmth, turning the day's food into heat. Light in the sky, light in the flame, warmth inside a person: a chain of light and heat. Chapter fifteen walks down that exact chain, and at every link Krishna says the same thing: that's me.
screen: `A CANDLE IN THE DARK.` → `THE MOON OVER THE STREET.` → `WARMTH INSIDE A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Still in the chariot, the two armies waiting, Krishna keeps teaching Arjuna. It starts with you. Verse seven: a fragment of me, eternal, became the living being in the world of life. Mamaivamsha: a part of my own self. Verse eight gives a gentle picture: when that living self takes a body and leaves it, it carries the senses along, the way the wind carries scent from a flower. You can't see it go, but something has moved. Then the chain of light. Verse twelve: the brightness in the sun that lights the whole world, the light in the moon, the light in fire: know that light as mine. Verse thirteen: entering the earth, I hold up all beings with my energy; becoming the juicy moon, soma, I nourish the plants. Verse fourteen: becoming the fire of digestion in living bodies, joined with the breath going in and out, I digest the four kinds of food. So in this chapter, the divine isn't only far off. Krishna says he is the warmth in the belly after dinner. Verse fifteen brings it all the way home: I am seated in the heart of all. From me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. Here is the teaching, plainly: for Hindus, God isn't only far above the world. God lives inside every being, the antaryami, the one within. And it's why so many Hindus, before eating, chant verse fourteen: aham vaishvanaro bhutva, I am the fire in living bodies. Dinner becomes an offering to the one already inside you.
screen: `A FRAGMENT OF ME, IN YOU.` · `LIGHT IN SUN, MOON AND FIRE.` · `THE FIRE THAT DIGESTS YOUR FOOD.` · `SEATED IN THE HEART OF ALL.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT IN THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, try what many Hindu families do: pause and offer it, silently or with the words aham vaishvanaro. If you don't pray, feel the warmth in your hands and belly and follow it back to the sun. Then rest at the center of your chest, where verse fifteen says the light is seated.
Tejas, brilliance, radiance. Gita fifteen, twelve: the brightness in the sun, the moon and the fire is Krishna's light; verse fifteen says that light is seated in every heart.
Your line: the divine light is seated in every heart. Krishna's words: sun, moon, fire, and the fire in you. See you at day two hundred twelve.

212.title: The highest person
212.hook: beyond what changes and what lasts: why Krishna is called Purushottama
212.carry: god is beyond both what changes and what lasts
212.howItsDone: Purushottama, the highest person, is a name of Krishna and Vishnu; some Hindus memorize Gita chapter fifteen, which names Purushottama near its close, and recite it whole.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tejas: the light in sun, moon and fire, and the divine light seated in every heart. Today, the chapter's last and shortest teaching.
screen: `TEJAS — THE LIGHT SEATED IN EVERY HEART.`

segments.voice: Krishna and Arjuna are still in the chariot, the two armies waiting. Krishna has just said his light is in the sun and in every heart. Now he goes further. Look at a wave. It rises, curls, crashes, and it's gone. The ocean under it doesn't crash; it was there before this wave and will be there after. The wave that passes, the water that stays. In five short verses, Krishna names those two, and then a third, beyond both. And he ends the chapter with a claim: know this, and you've done what you came to do.
screen: `THE WAVE THAT PASSES.` → `THE WATER THAT STAYS.` → `AND ONE BEYOND BOTH.`

segments.voice: Verse sixteen. There are two persons in this world, the perishable and the imperishable. Kshara, the perishable, is all beings: every body, every life that begins and ends. Akshara, the imperishable, is called kutastha, the one that stands firm, unchanging. Verse seventeen: but the highest person is another, called the supreme self, the undying Lord who enters the three worlds and holds them up. Verse eighteen: because I am beyond the perishable, and higher even than the imperishable, I am known in the world and in the Veda as Purushottama, the highest person. Purushottama is still a name for Krishna and Vishnu. Here the schools read carefully and differently. For Ramanuja and his school, the three are real and distinct: changing beings, unchanging souls, and the Lord beyond and within both. For Advaita teachers, the highest person is the one reality, and the other two are how it appears to us. Verse nineteen: whoever, free of confusion, knows me as the highest person, knows everything, and worships me with their whole being. Verse twenty ends the chapter: this is the most secret teaching, Arjuna. Knowing this, a person becomes wise, and has done all there is to do. Here is the teaching, plainly: for Hindus, God isn't one more thing in the world, and isn't only the quiet self inside you. God holds both, and is beyond both. So when a Hindu bows to Krishna, they turn toward what holds everything that changes and everything that lasts.

segments.voice: Notice what's changing: the breath, sounds arriving and leaving, thoughts passing; that's the perishable. Then notice what hasn't changed since you sat down, the plain fact of being aware, which is closer to the unchanging. Without trying to picture anything, rest your attention on whatever holds both; you don't have to name it, just let the sitting be wide enough to include it.
Purushottama, the highest person. Gita fifteen: the perishable and the imperishable, and beyond both, Purushottama, higher even than the imperishable.

213.title: Fearlessness first
213.hook: Krishna's list of divine qualities starts with fearlessness, for an Arjuna who dropped his bow
213.carry: fearlessness is the first divine quality
213.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 16.1–16.3 as a list of virtues to cultivate, opening with abhaya (fearlessness); many murtis and images of the gods show abhaya mudra, the raised open palm that says 'do not fear'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, purushottama: the perishable, the imperishable, and the highest person beyond both. Today, a list that starts somewhere unexpected.

Go back to where the Gita began. Arjuna stands in his chariot between two armies and sees his teachers, cousins and uncles on the other side. His limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, his great bow Gandiva slips from his hand, and he sinks down, overcome with grief. Fifteen chapters later, Krishna gives him a list: the qualities of someone born to a divine inheritance. And the very first word, before truth, before compassion, is abhaya. Fearlessness. Why?
screen: `ARJUNA DROPS HIS BOW.` → `FIFTEEN CHAPTERS LATER, A LIST.` → `THE FIRST WORD: FEARLESSNESS.`

segments.voice: Verses one to three are one long sentence. Fearlessness. Purity of heart. Steadiness in knowledge and practice. Giving. Self-control. Sacrifice. Study of scripture. Discipline. Straightness. Then: doing no harm, truth, freedom from anger, letting go, peace, not gossiping about others, kindness to all beings, not being greedy, gentleness, modesty, not being fickle. And to close: energy, forgiveness, endurance, cleanliness, no malice, no excess pride. Twenty-six in all. Krishna calls them daivi sampad, the divine inheritance, like a fortune you're born into. Why fearlessness first? The text doesn't say. One answer teachers give: without it, the others don't hold. It's hard to tell the truth if you're afraid, hard to forgive, to give, to stay gentle. Fear quietly bends everything else. The second word, sattva-samshuddhi, purity of heart, is about what's underneath: clean motives, not only clean hands. Together they make today's line. Verse four gives the opposite list, briefly: hypocrisy, arrogance, too much pride, anger, harshness and ignorance. Tomorrow, that side. Verse five: the divine inheritance leads to freedom, the other to bondage. Then Krishna turns to Arjuna, who began this whole conversation overcome with grief, and says something gentle: do not grieve, Arjuna. You were born to the divine inheritance. The inheritance is already his. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, fearlessness isn't toughness. It grows from knowing who you are, the self that, as chapter two said, no weapon can cut. It's why so many images of the gods show one palm raised toward you: abhaya mudra, the gesture that says, do not fear.
screen: `TWENTY-SIX QUALITIES.` · `FEARLESSNESS FIRST.` · `PURITY OF HEART UNDERNEATH.` · `DON'T GRIEVE. IT'S ALREADY HIS.` · `ABHAYA MUDRA: DO NOT FEAR.` · then, large: `FEARLESSNESS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Picture an image of a Hindu god with the right palm raised toward you, abhaya mudra: do not fear. Then find one small fear you're carrying, a conversation you're avoiding, and hold it in front of that open hand. Breathe in and feel where it sits; breathe out and let it soften. If you pray, ask for courage; if you don't, ask quietly: if this fear were smaller, what would I do?
Abhaya, fearlessness, no fear. Gita sixteen, one to five: the first of twenty-six qualities of the divine inheritance, daivi sampad, alongside purity of heart.
Your line: fearlessness is the first divine quality. Courage first, a clean heart underneath. Day two hundred thirteen, in the books.

214.title: The three gates
214.hook: the Gita's 'demonic' is a way of living, entered by desire, anger and greed
214.carry: desire, anger and greed, the three gates of hell
214.howItsDone: At Navratri and Durga Puja many Hindus remember Durga's victory over the asura Mahishasura; teachers often read Gita 16 as a mirror for self-examination rather than a way to label others, and the three gates of 16.21, kama, krodha and lobha, are widely quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhaya: fearlessness, the first divine quality, with purity of heart underneath. Today, the other list.

Hear the word demonic and you probably picture horns, fire, a horror movie. The Gita's picture is quieter, and more unsettling. It's a person lying awake at night, running the numbers. I got this today. Tomorrow I'll get that. This is mine, and that will be mine too. I beat that rival, and I'll beat the others. Who is like me? It sounds less like a monster and more like a very busy, very anxious person. Maybe someone most of us have been, for an evening or two.
screen: `NOT HORNS AND FIRE.` → `SOMEONE AWAKE, RUNNING THE NUMBERS.` → `WHO IS LIKE ME?`

segments.voice: Verse six: there are two kinds of beings in this world, the divine and the asuric, usually translated demonic. In Hindu stories the asuras are the gods' rivals, powerful and proud, like Mahishasura, the buffalo demon who seized heaven and still wanted more, until the Goddess Durga brought him down, the victory many Hindus celebrate at Navratri. Here the word describes a way of living. Verses seven and eight: such people don't know when to act and when to hold back. They say the world has no truth, no ground, no God, and runs on desire alone. Verse ten: gripped by desire that can never be filled, full of hypocrisy, pride and arrogance. Then verses twelve to fifteen, the monologue from the hook. Bound by hundreds of hopes, they pile up wealth by any means. This I gained today, this wish I'll fulfill. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, strong and happy. Who else is like me? Even their rituals, verse seventeen says, are done for show. The Gita's verdict is severe: this road leads downward, again and again. Many teachers, especially modern ones, read this chapter less as a label for other people and more as a mirror, though some classical commentators read it as a portrait of a kind of soul. Then verse twenty-one names where it all starts: three gates to hell that destroy the self. Kama, desire; krodha, anger; and lobha, greed. Shut those three, the Gita says, and a person begins to walk toward the highest. That's the teaching: the gates aren't groups of people. They're three movements inside anyone.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF BEINGS.` · `THIS IS MINE. WHO IS LIKE ME?` · `A MIRROR, NOT A LABEL.` · `DESIRE, ANGER, GREED.` · then, large: `THE THREE GATES.`

segments.voice: Listen for the monologue: something to get, someone to beat, something that's mine. Don't argue with it; just hear it, the way you'd hear a radio in another room. Then check the three gates, desire pulling, anger simmering, a grasping for more, and wherever one is open, breathe out slowly and let it close a little.
The demonic. Gita sixteen: the asuric way of living, restless, proud and grasping, and the three gates that lead there: desire, anger and greed.
Your line: desire, anger and greed, the three gates of hell. Shut them, the Gita says, and you start toward the highest. Two hundred fourteen days in.

215.title: Steer by the teaching
215.hook: Arjuna asks to be taught; the Gita says steer by scripture, not desire
215.carry: let the teaching, not desire, be your measure
215.howItsDone: Some Hindus look to shastra, the Vedas and the texts that follow them as taught by a guru or family tradition, for guidance on ritual and conduct; Gita 16.24 is quoted for scripture as the measure of right action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the demonic: the monologue of this is mine, who is like me, and three gates, desire, anger, greed. Today, what to steer by instead.

Go back to chapter two. Arjuna is sitting in his chariot, refusing to fight, sure of what he feels and sure of nothing else. Then he says something brave: my mind is confused about my duty. I am your student. Teach me. That's where the whole Gita starts: not with Arjuna following his feelings, and not with blind obedience, but with a student asking for a chart. Chapter sixteen closes the loop: steer by the wind of whatever you want right now, or by a chart people before you drew.
screen: `ARJUNA: I AM YOUR STUDENT.` → `TEACH ME.` → `THE WIND, OR A CHART?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-two picks up yesterday's three gates. Whoever is free of those three doors of darkness does what is good for their own self, and goes to the highest. Verse twenty-three: whoever throws aside the rule of scripture and acts on the pull of desire reaches neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal. And verse twenty-four, the chapter's last word: so let scripture be your measure in deciding what to do and what not to do. Know what the rule says, and act in this world. The word is shastra: teaching, a rule, a manual, sometimes a whole science. There are shastras for grammar, music, and how to live. Here the contrast isn't scripture against thinking. It's scripture against kama, desire, the first of yesterday's gates. Desire is a poor compass; it points to itself. Hindus read this verse in more than one way. For some, the shastra is the Vedas and the texts that follow them, learned from a teacher. Others stress that the Gita itself is a shastra, and that knowing the rule means understanding its purpose, not just its letter. That's why, in Hindu families, big choices, a wedding date, a child's name, a vow, are often taken to a guru, a priest or an elder who knows the texts: not to switch off thinking, but to borrow a chart older than your wants. And look what comes next. Chapter seventeen opens with Arjuna asking: what about people who don't follow the scripture's rules, but who worship with real faith? The Gita takes it up in the very next verse.
screen: `FREE OF THE THREE GATES.` · `DESIRE IS A POOR COMPASS.` · `LET SCRIPTURE BE YOUR MEASURE.` · `SHASTRA: TEACHING, RULE, MANUAL.` · then, large: `STEER BY THE TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Think of one decision on your mind, and let desire speak first: what do I want, right this minute? Then ask what the best teaching you know would say, a verse, a grandparent's rule, something from these two hundred days. If you pray, ask, as Arjuna did, to be taught. Hold both answers side by side without choosing yet, and just see the difference.
Shastra, teaching, rule, authoritative text. Gita sixteen, twenty-four: let it be your measure for what to do and not do, rather than the pull of desire.

216.title: Made of faith
216.hook: can faith without the books count? Arjuna asks, and Krishna answers
216.carry: a person is made of their faith
216.howItsDone: Shraddha, faith as trust and wholehearted commitment, is a key word in Hindu practice; Gita 17.3, 'a person is made of faith', is quoted by teachers to explain why sincere practice shapes a person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shastra: let the teaching, not desire, be your measure. And Arjuna had a question waiting.

A grandmother who never read the books. She couldn't recite a single verse in Sanskrit, but she lit the lamp every evening, for as long as anyone can remember, and never once missed it. She didn't know the rules. But she had something. Arjuna has just heard Krishna say, let scripture be your measure. His next question could be about people like her. Chapter seventeen opens with it. What about them, Krishna? The ones who set aside the rules, but worship with faith?
screen: `SHE NEVER READ THE BOOKS.` → `A LAMP LIT EVERY EVENING.` → `WHAT ABOUT HER FAITH?`

segments.voice: Verse one is Arjuna's question: those who set aside the rule of scripture but worship full of faith, what is their standing? Sattva, rajas or tamas? He's using the three threads from chapter fourteen. Krishna doesn't say those people are wrong. Verse two: faith comes in three kinds, born of each person's own nature. Then verse three. Everyone's faith takes the shape of their inner being. A person is made of faith. Shraddhamayo 'yam purushah. Whatever their faith is, that's what they are. Yo yac-chraddhah sa eva sah. Not: a person has a faith. A person is made of it. The word is shraddha, often translated faith. Some teachers take it apart as shrat, truth or the heart, and dha, to place: placing your heart. So it's less about believing a list of statements, more about where you set your trust. Then the chapter begins to sort. Verse four: the clear-hearted worship the gods; the restless worship yakshas and rakshasas, spirits of wealth and power; the heavy worship ghosts. Verses five and six warn about people who torture their own bodies with harsh practices the scriptures never taught, full of show and ego. They hurt the body, Krishna says, and me, who lives inside it. So for Hindus, faith isn't a test you pass by knowing the verses. Many teachers read it this way: you become what you place your heart in, which is why a grandmother's lamp, lit every evening, matters.
screen: `WHAT ABOUT FAITH WITHOUT RULES?` · `FAITH COMES IN THREE KINDS.` · `A PERSON IS MADE OF FAITH.` · `NO SHOW, NO SELF-TORTURE.` · then, large: `MADE OF FAITH.`

segments.voice: Ask gently: where do I place my heart? Not what I say I believe, but what I actually trust, day to day: a person, a routine, money, a practice, God, my own effort. No answer is wrong; just notice which ones rise first, and how each one feels in the body.
Shraddha, faith, trust. Gita seventeen, three: each person's faith takes the shape of their nature; a person is made of it, and as their faith is, so are they.
Your line: a person is made of their faith. As your faith is, so you become. See you tomorrow.

217.title: Food and the gift
217.hook: Krishna refuses a prince's feast for a humble meal; the Gita's three kinds of food and gift
217.carry: sattvic food, and the gift that wants nothing back
217.howItsDone: Many Hindus cook fresh, simple, sattvic food for an offering and offer it to God before eating (some avoid onion and garlic, especially for offerings); Gita 17.20's gift given without hope of return is cited in teaching on dana, charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shraddha: a person is made of faith, and faith follows nature. Today, the three threads come to the table.

Before the war, Krishna goes to Hastinapura to try for peace. Prince Duryodhana has a royal feast ready for him, hoping to win him over. Krishna turns it down. A person eats another's food, he says, when it's offered with love or when they're in need, and neither is true here. He walks to the house of Vidura, a humble, honest man, and eats there. Later, on the battlefield, the Gita sorts four ordinary things into three kinds: what you eat, how you worship, how you discipline yourself, and how you give.
screen: `A PRINCE'S FEAST, REFUSED.` → `A HUMBLE MEAL AT VIDURA'S.` → `THREE KINDS OF FOOD.`

segments.voice: Food first. Verse eight: sattvic food lengthens life and brings purity, strength, health, happiness and cheer. It's tasty, smooth, nourishing and pleasant. Verse nine: rajasic food is bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry and burning. It brings pain, grief and sickness. Verse ten: tamasic food is stale, flavorless, spoiled, leftover, impure. Some commentators read that 'very' as reaching across the whole list, so the trouble is excess, not flavor. Then sacrifice, the offering. Sattvic: done because it ought to be done, not for a reward. Rajasic: done for the reward, or for show. Tamasic: done carelessly, without faith, without the proper words, without sharing food with others. Then austerity, tapas, discipline, in three places. Of the body: honoring teachers, cleanliness, doing no harm. Of speech, verse fifteen: words that don't upset people, that are true, kind and helpful. Of the mind: calm, gentleness, silence, self-control. Done with faith and no wish for reward, it's sattvic. Done for honor and praise, rajasic. Done to torture yourself or harm someone else, tamasic. And last, the gift. Verse twenty: a gift given simply because it should be given, to someone who can't pay you back, at the right time and place, to the right person, is sattvic. Given to get something back, or grudgingly: rajasic. Given with contempt, at the wrong time, to the wrong person: tamasic. That's why many Hindus cook fresh, simple food to offer to God before anyone eats, and why dana, the gift that wants nothing back, is honored as the highest giving.
screen: `FOOD: NOURISHING, TOO MUCH, STALE.` · `SACRIFICE: DUTY, SHOW, CARELESS.` · `AUSTERITY OF BODY, SPEECH, MIND.` · `THE GIFT THAT WANTS NOTHING BACK.` · then, large: `FOOD AND THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, do what many Hindu families do: offer the plate first, in words or in your heart, and eat what comes back as prasad. If you don't pray, just notice whether this food will leave you light, buzzing, or heavy. Then hold in mind one small gift you could give someone who can't repay you, and give it this week.
Food. Gita seventeen: food, sacrifice, austerity and gift each come in three kinds, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, and the kind shapes the one who eats, offers or gives.
